title: Ag Nanoparticle Embedded Cu Nanoporous Hybrid Arrays for the Selective Electrocatalytic Reduction of CO2 towards Ethylene
abstract: Electrocatalytic reduction of carbon dioxide (CO2RR) driven by renewable electricity is a promising strategy for chemical recycling of carbon. It can alleviate the carbon emission by reducing the carbon dioxide concentrations in the atmosphere, transforming low energy density renewable energy into high energy density carbonaceous fuels. Copper-based catalysts play an important role in the field of electrocatalytic CO2 because of their ability to reduce CO2 to hydrocarbons. However, problems such as high overpotential, catalyst deactivation, and uncontrollable product selectivity limit their further development. Herein, we construct Ag/Cu and Zn/Cu composite structures for CO2 reduction by employing tiny Ag nanoparticles and Zn nanocones uniformly distributed on the surface of porous network Cu nanowires. It is found that Ag/Cu composite structures are more active for the reduction of CO2 to C2H4, compared to those of Zn modified. The Faraday efficiency of CO2 reduction to ethylene reaches up to 41.3% and it remains stable for more than 8 hours. Theoretical calculations show that the modification of silver regulates the electronic structure of highly porous copper at the Cu/Ag interface, accelerate the process of carbon dioxide reduction of the first electron, enhanced the adsorption of *CO and further facilitated *CO dimerization to ethylene. Therefore, the strategy of silver-modified porous copper pre-catalyst is a promising approach for CO2 reduction to hydrocarbons.

sections.text:
Electrocatalytic reduction of carbon dioxide (CO2RR) driven by renewable electricity is a promising strategy for chemical recycling of carbon. It can alleviate the carbon emission by reducing the carbon dioxide concentrations in the atmosphere, transforming low energy density renewable energy into high energy density carbonaceous fuels. Copper-based catalysts play an important role in the field of electrocatalytic CO2 because of their ability to reduce CO2 to hydrocarbons. However, problems such as high overpotential, catalyst deactivation, and uncontrollable product selectivity limit their further development. Herein, we construct Ag/Cu and Zn/Cu composite structures for CO2 reduction by employing tiny Ag nanoparticles and Zn nanocones uniformly distributed on the surface of porous network Cu nanowires. It is found that Ag/Cu composite structures are more active for the reduction of CO2 to C2H4, compared to those of Zn modified. The Faraday efficiency of CO2 reduction to ethylene reaches up to 41.3% and it remains stable for more than 8 hours. Theoretical calculations show that the modification of silver regulates the electronic structure of highly porous copper at the Cu/Ag interface, accelerate the process of carbon dioxide reduction of the first electron, enhanced the adsorption of *CO and further facilitated *CO dimerization to ethylene. Therefore, the strategy of silver-modified porous copper pre-catalyst is a promising approach for CO2 reduction to hydrocarbons.
Key words：Nanoporous copper, Ethylene, CO2 reduction, High efficiency

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text:
The electrochemical reduction of carbon dioxide driven by renewable energy converts carbon dioxide into value-added chemicals or fuels to solve the problems of depletion of fossil fuels and excessive carbon emissions, which is of great significance to the sustainability of human society.[1-5] Although thermodynamics indicates that electrochemical reduction of carbon dioxide is feasible, slow kinetics make it impractical unless exploring efficient catalysts that enhance Faraday efficiency and reduce energy consumption. [6-7] Today, common catalysts for CO2 electrolytic reduction are based on transition metals and their compounds. For instance, noble metals such as Au, Ag and Pd[8-10] reduce CO2 to CO at a moderate overpotential; non-noble metals such as Sn, In and Bi[11-13] have high selectivity for formic acid; Zn exhibits good catalytic properties for CO, HCOOH and syngas at different overpotentials.[14-18] Particularly, Cu is the most effective catalyst that can deeply reduce CO2 to hydrocarbon fuels, including methanol, methane and ethylene, where ethylene is known as an important industrial gas and has a high energy density.[7,19] However, the copper catalyst was found to have a lower Faraday efficiency for hydrocarbons with high energy density.[20-21] Therefore, the development of new copper-containing catalysts with enhanced intrinsic activity and selectivity for hydrocarbons is a very challenging research work.
CO2 reduction is very complicated, involving multiple electrons and proton coupling
steps, so the reaction pathway and the final product depend on the binding energy of key intermediates on the catalyst surface.[22] The selectivity of the product can be manipulated by changing and improving the morphology, surface state and chemical and phase composition of the catalyst. Previous studies have shown that roughened copper surfaces (such as Cu derived from Cu2O) can reduce CO2 to ethylene (C2H4) and ethanol with a Faraday efficiency of greater than 45%[23] and three-dimensional nanoporous copper morphology also has good catalytic performance for ethylene production (38% Faraday efficiency).[24] Recently, an effective method has been reported to increase the selectivity and reactivity of copper by combining a second metal to adjust the bonding strength of intermediates on the catalytic surface.[25] Ma et al. reported that the phase-separated Cu/Pd catalyst achieved good selectivity for ethylene.[26] Huang et al. also observed that Cu/Ag nanocrystals had a good catalytic performance in promoting CO2RR to ethylene.[27] Ma et al. demonstrated Cu/Zn bimetallic catalysts can change the selectivity of CO2RR towards ethanol.[28] Therefore, bimetallic catalysts are effective for the multi-carbon production of CO2 electroreduction.

Hence, it is expected the second metal can substantially activate Cu to multicarbon products by “tandem catalysis” mechanisms.[32-35] Specifically, CO intermediates can first form at the second metallic sites, which will then be transferred to adjacent Cu sites where they would further evolve into hydrocarbon products.
Here, we demonstrate the effect of modifying the second metal component by
constructing Ag@Cu, Zn@Cu composite structure with tiny Ag nanoparticles and Zn nanocones uniformly distributed on the surface of porous network Cu nanowires. As expected, the composite structure has excellent catalytic activity for the CO2 reduction, and the modification of Ag nanoparticle makes the Faraday efficiency of ethylene reach 41.3% at the potential of -1.2V RHE. In addition, the high Faraday efficiency can be maintained for 8 hours without a significant decrease, indicating its long-term stability. DFT calculation reveals that the enhancement is the result of tandem catalysis and electronic effect, both induced by the coupling of nanoscale segregated the second nanometal and Cu domains through an interfacial region. Experimental Chemicals
All chemicals and solvents were used as received without any further purification. Copper coil (Cu,99.99%) and silvernitrate (AgNO3,99.99%) were bought from Sigma Aldrich. Copper sulfate pentahydrate (CuSO4·5H2O) was obtained from J & K chemical. Zinc nitrate hexahydrate (Zn(NO)3*6H2O,99.9%) and 3,5-diamino-1,2,4-triazole (DAT,99.9%) were purchased from Alfa Aesar. Ascorbic acid (C6H8O6, AR grade), sulfuric acid (H2SO4,98%) and phosphoric acid (H3PO485%) were obtained from Sinopharm Chemical Reagent. potassium hydrogen carbonate (KHCO3, 99.99%) were bought from Macklin. Carbon dioxide (CO2, 99.999%) and nitrogen (N2, 99.9999%) were supplied by Beijing Beiwen Gases Company. Deionized water used in all experiments was with a resistivity of 18.2 MΩ. Nanoporous Copper (Cu Np) Nanoporous copper was electrodeposited on the electropolished Cu foils using galvanostatic deposition. The samples were electrodeposited 300 s at a constant current of 4 mA in an electroplating bath made of 0.1 M CuSO4·5H2O,10mM 3,5-diamino-1,2,4-triazole (DAT) and 10mM Ammonium citrate at pH = 1.5 adjusted by using H2SO4.[36] The Pt mesh is used as a counter electrode. The Ag/AgCl reference electrode is placed near the working electrode to measure the potential. Ag@Cu Np and Zn@Cu Np hybrid arrays The Ag@Cu Np hybrid array sample was synthesized by sequential precipitation (SP)on the nanoporous copper at room temperature. Firstly, Spin coating 0.6 mol/L ascorbic acid solution on the nanoporous copper foil at 3000 rpm for 30 seconds. Then spin coating the solution containing 0.5 mmol/L AgNO3 at 3000 rpm for 1 minute. After standing for 2 minutes, the sample was washed with deionized water to remove the excess amount of salt solution, followed by drying in vacuum. The preparation of Zn@Cu Np is the same as this method, except that the second spin coating solution is replaced by 0.5 mmol/L Zn
(NO3)2 · 6H2O, the sample was then washed with deionized water to remove excess salt solution, dried in vacuum . Characterization of pre-catalysts
The surface morphologies of the Cu pre-catalysts were characterized by SEM (FEI
Quanta 3D) at an accelerating voltage of 5 kV. The crystal structure and detailed information about the morphology of the samples were obtained using TEM (JEM-120F). STEM images were implemented by the JEOL JEM 2100F electron microscope. XRD measurements were performed on a Rigaku TTRIII X-ray diffractometer using a Cu Kα radiation source (λ = 1.54056 Å) to determine the crystal structure and phase. The chemical states of molybdenum and sulfur were measured by a Thermo Scientific ESCA Lab 250Xi XPS photo-electron spectrometer with a monochromatic Al Kα source (hν =1486.6 eV). three-electrode cell configuration with an Ag/AgCl (3.5 M KCl) reference electrode and a Pt mesh counter electrode. A gas-tight, two-component electrochemical cell was adopted to conduct the CO2 reduction experiments. The anodic and cathodic compartments were

Each electrode compartment was filled with 50 ml of electrolyte leaving approximately 35 ml of headspace. An aqueous 0.5 M KHCO3 (pH 7.2) solution was used as the electrolyte and was saturated with CO2 gas for at least 30 minutes before each measurement. The electrolyte in the cathode chamber was rotated at a rate of 350 rpm with a magnetic stirrer throughout the electrolysis process. During the electrolysis, CO2 was continuously pumped into the catholyte at a rate of 30 mL/min using a calibrated mass flow controller. All experiments were performed at 298 K. The CV curves were obtained in the electrolyte saturated with CO2 between the scanning interval of −0.6V (vs. Ag/AgCl) and −2.0 V (vs. Ag/AgCl) at the scan rate of 50 mV/s. All potentials were converted to the reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE) reference scale through the following equation:
E (vs. RHE) = E (vs. Ag/AgCl) + 0.205 + 0.059 * pH
The gas outlet of the cathode chamber was connected to a gas-sampling loop of a gas
chromatograph (GC, Shimadzu GC-2014C) equipped with a packed Molecular Sieve 5A capillary column (Agilent) and a Porapak Q column (Agilent, 80-100 mesh). A thermal conductivity detector (TCD) and a flame ionization detector (FID) were installed on the GC to detect escaping gas products. The carrier gases for TCD and FID are nitrogen and helium, respectively. The GC was periodically calibrated with standard gas mixtures under standard conditions (1 atm, 298 K). The liquid products were determined by 1H NMR (Bruker Advance 400 spectrometer, 400 MHz). 0.9 mL of electrolyte was mixed with 2.0 ppm of dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) and 0.1 mL of D2O was added as an internal standard. The Faradaic efficiency (η) was calculated from the concentrations as follows：
η = ppm × flow rate × (nFp0/RT) × (jTot)-1 × 100%
Where ppm is the concentration of gas determined by GC, n is the electron transfer number, F is the Faradaic constant, p0 is the pressure, T = 273.15K and jTot is the total current density. The calibrated partial current density of products was obtained by the following equitation:
jpart = jTot × η(product)
At the same time, liquid products were quantified using 1H NMR spectroscopy
(Ascend-400). Typically, 0.5 mL of electrolyte was sampled at the conclusion of the electrolysis was mixed with 0.1 mL D2O, and 1.67 ppm dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) was added as the internal standard. Density functional theory calculations All electronic structure calculations were performed by density functional theory with the Vienna Ab initio simulation package (VASP). We chose Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof (PBE) functionals and the projector-augmented wave (PAW) method. Calculations were carried out on the basis of the obtained equilibrium lattice constants of Ag and Cu unit cell with full relaxation using a plane-wave cut-off of 400 eV. The Cu surface exhibits well-defined (100) planes exposed (Fig. S1). The 2 Ag atoms or 2 Zn atoms were placed on 4x4 unit Cu (100) slab (Fig. S2). The structures of the bulk and extended surface were fully relaxed until the force on any atom was smaller than 0.03 eV/Å. A minimum of 5 × 5 × 5 k-points was used in the Brillouin zone of the conventional cell for bulk and 3 × 3 × 1 k-points for surface. A vacuum layer of over 15 Å was used to avoid the interaction with image atoms. Results and discussion
The synthesis process of Ag nanoparticle embedded Cu nanoporous hybrid arrays
(Ag@Cu Np) is as follows. Firstly, Cu Np was synthesized on cleaned electropolished copper foil by an electrodeposition method (for more information, see the experimental section). During the electrodeposition, Cu2+ in the electrolyte was reduced to metallic Cu at the Cu foil surface and deposited to form Cu nanopores via the electrocrystallization process. Subsequently, Ag NPs were embedded on the surface of Cu Np by the in situ reduction method using silver nitrate as the Ag source. It is worth noting that although Ag+ could be reduced to metallic Ag by Cu through the displacement reaction (Cu0 + 2Ag+ → Cu2+ + 2Ag), ascorbic acid was necessary to be added into the solution as a reducing agent to reduce Ag+ and Cu2+ in the vicinity of Cu nanopores into metallic ones. Zn@Cu Np was prepared in the same manner except that zinc nitrate hexahydrate was used as a zinc source during the reduction process.

Cu Np consists of an interconnected three-dimensional network structure with copper-frame nanowires width of 40 ± 10 nm (Fig. 1a, d, Fig. 2c), these nanowires greatly enhance the specific surface area and expose a large number of catalytic active sites. It is observed at low magnification that Ag@Cu Np and Zn@Cu Np still retain a good Cu nanoporous structure (Fig. 1b, c). Ag is uniformly distributed in the form of particles size on the porous copper skeleton nanowires at low magnification (Fig. 1e), [30] and its particle size is mainly distributed between 30-50 nm (Fig. 2d). While zinc is embedded in the Cu nanoporous in the form of submicron pyramids, the size of which is not uniform, ranging from several tens of nanometers to 1 micrometer (Fig. 1f). The transmission electron microscopy (TEM) image (Fig. 2a, S3, S4) shows that Ag particles are combined together tightly with Cu nanowires. From the high resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) image of Ag@Cu Np (Fig. 2b), the lattice spacing of Ag (111) and Cu (111) are measured to be 0.237 and 0.208 nm respectively, which are very close to that of face-centered cubic Ag (111) (0.238 nm) and Cu (111) (0.209 nm), indicating that Ag nanoparticle is embedded in Cu nanoporous structures. These Ag nanoparticles are easily activated as sites for catalytic reactions.[37]

X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns of Cu Np, Ag@Cu Np and Zn@Cu Np are shown in
Fig. 3a. Only Cu diffraction peaks of (111), (200), and (220) facets are present for the four samples, indicating the content of Ag and Zn is very low and below the detection limit. Notably, compared with Cu foil, the diffraction peaks of (111), (200), and (220) facets in Ag@Cu Np and Zn@Cu Np shift of ≈0.09°to lower diffraction angles, respectively, which
is ascribed to the substitution of Cu atoms by Ag atoms with bigger diameter in Ag@Cu Np and lattice expansion occurs (Fig. S5). The composition information of the as-prepared Ag@Cu Np and Zn@Cu is exhibited in Fig. 3b. A dominant peak at 935.3 eV corresponding to Cu0 or Cu+ is discerned for Cu Np. The presence of satellite peak at 944.1 eV in all the three samples suggests the existence of Cu2+ species.[38-40] The Cu2+ and Cu+ species in Cu Np should come from oxidation of the surface upon exposure to the air. However, the major peak in Ag@Cu Np and Zn@Cu Np displays broadened FWHMs and slightly positively shifts respectively. This is due to the increased surface Cu2+ concentration at the expense of Cu0 resulted from the introduction of Ag or Zn on the surface.[32] The Cu2+ species own broader FWHM and more positive binding energy compared with Cu0 species. The Zn spectra between Zn@Cu Np and Cu Np are totally different (Fig. 3c). The peaks at 1045.1 eV and 1021.6 eV of Zn@Cu Np correspond to Zn2+ species.[41] Meanwhile,the Ag spectra of Ag@Cu Np and Cu Np are also different (Fig. 3d). The peaks at 374.1 eV and 368.1eV of Ag@Cu Np correspond to Ag0 species.[42] XPS spectra verify the successful modification of silver and zinc on the surface of nanoporous copper.
Electrocatalytic CO2RR performance was tested in a CO2 saturated 0.5 M KHCO3 aqueous solution in a typical three-electrode H-type cell. To examine the CO2RR catalytic activity, linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) was firstly conducted at a sweep rate of 50 mV/s. As shown in Fig. 4a, the Ag@Cu Np exhibits a high current density of −19.61 mA cm−2 at −1.2V, which is higher than that of Cu Np, Zn@Cu Np and copper foil, indicating Ag@Cu Np pre-catalyst has high activity toward CO2RR. The CO2 reduction total current density of Zn@Cu Np is also increased compared to Cu Np and copper foil. The CO2RR products are quantified using online gas chromatography and a 1H nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectrometer (Fig. S6). To analyze the selectivity toward CO2 reduction product with different applied potentials, the Faradaic efficiency (Fig.4b, c) for all gas and liquid products over the Ag@Cu Np and Zn@Cu Np pre-catalysts shows the same change trend as a function of the applied potential. In detail, it can be found that the CO2RR carbonaceous products on the pre-catalysts are C2H4, HCOOH, and CO. Besides, H2 is also detected due to the

To test the operational stability of the pre-catalysts, we carried out CO2RR reduction over an extended period. Being continuously electrolyzed for 8 h of CO2RR, the Ag@Cu Np exhibits relatively stable current density and Faradaic efficiency of C2H4, and then there is a downward trend (Fig. S10). By contrast, the stability performance of the Zn@Cu Np pre-catalyst in KHCO3 aqueous solution also shows a highly competitive advantage. Moreover, the Ag@Cu Np also keeps its original morphology after the stability test (Fig. S11). This stability can be owning to its negligible selectivity toward methane, which is reported to be related to the formation of graphitic carbon poisons. To shed light on the kinetic mechanism of the CO2RR to C2H4 over the Ag@Cu Np and Zn@Cu Np pre-catalyst, a plot of the log of the partial current density versus the potential for C2H4 production (Tafel plot) was obtained by stepped-potential electrolysis.[43] As shown in Fig. 5, Ag@Cu Np shows a Tafel slope of 122 mV dec−1, a value consistent with the mechanistic hypothesis that the formation of CO2*- intermediate from the initial e- transfer is the possible rate-determining step.[44] In contrast, Cu foil exhibits a higher Tafel slope of 228 mV dec-1, indicating that its reaction kinetics is significantly weaker than that of Ag@Cu Np, which is likely due to the better stabilization of CO2*- intermediate by the Cu nanopartcles. The Tafel slope of Zn@Cu Np is less than that of Cu Np, suggesting that the embedded Zn submicron pyramids on Zn@Cu Np could also effectively promote C2H4 formation, but the catalytic effect is not as significant as that of Ag.

The comprehensive mechanism of CO2 or CO electroreduction to C2 species might vary directly with the exposed facets, solvents, and other factors.[45-47] The previous work[27] reported that the trends in C2H4 production was caused by a tandem catalysis mechanism, where Ag NPs reduced CO2 to CO near the Cu surface, driven by a high *CO coverage, and the Cu surface further reduced CO to C2H4. To further understand the reaction mechanism of the CO2RR over Cu Np, Ag@Cu Np and Zn@Cu Np, we conducted density functional theory (DFT) calculations. The Gibbs free energy profiles of CO2 reduction to C2H4 over Cu surfaces (100) facets were calculated.[47] It was widely accepted that *CO is a key intermediate for producing hydrocarbons by the electroreduction of CO2. DFT calculations show that the CO binding energy of Ag (Ag ad = −2.26 eV) is higher than that of Zn (Znad = −1.71 eV) and Cu (Cu ad = −1.53 eV). Therefore, once the CO molecules form on Cu atoms, they may be captured by Ag or Zn atoms, stay in the Ag/Cu or Zn/Cu interface. It facilitates the enrichment of large amounts of *CO intermediates on the copper surface. It is well known that both Ag and Zn favor producing CO as the final product as they have weak adsorbing energy toward *CO, while Cu prefers to generate C2 products since its moderate adsorption energy to *CO. From the thermodynamic view, *CO can be better stabilized at Cu surface. Thus, the locally generated CO at Zn or Ag can be furnished to Cu via surface diffusion over nanoscale or increasing the local concentration within CO diffusion boundary layer. And only the at the interface, the resulted enhanced *CO coverage on Cu will promote C2 evolution by C-C coupling reaction.[26,31] However, due to the diffusion gradient, the *CO concentration at the Cu surface is lower than that at the interface. It will show lower C2 generation rate compared with that at the interface.
In the following steps toward ethylene, a rate-determining step (RDS) is the formation
C-C bond via *CO dimerization. It has been reported that the electroreduction of CO2 toward CO on Cu was a facile process.[48] Moreover, both the CO and CO2 reduction on Cu give similar product distribution, which further demonstrate that CO is a crucial intermediate and the RDS for C2+ product generation is later than the CO evolution.[49,50] And it is well accepted that the *CO-*CO dimerization reaction is the RDS as reported by many literatures.[37,51] A prerequisite for CO dimerization is the existence of much closely contacted *CO, otherwise, the CO will evolve into C1 products. Next, the *CO-*CO dimerization is mediated by electron transfer, rendering a *OCCO- intermediate, and continuous coupling proton-electron transfer into the intermediates leads to protonation and dehydration, eventually giving rise to the ethylene molecules. The energy barrier of C-C coupling during the formation of ethylene is critical because it is the only endothermic process and the rate-limiting step of the CO2 reduction (Fig. 6c). The formation of *OCCO- is more favorable on the Ag@Cu Np surface due to the minimum ∆G values (0.36 eV) among Cu Np and Zn@Cu Np. sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: In summary, the Ag@Cu Np and Zn@Cu Np nanocomposites for CO2 reduction were successfully prepared by a simple two-step process, respectively. The Ag/Cu composites present excellent catalytic activity and exhibit a maximum C2H4 Faradaic efficiency of ∼41.3% at −1.2 V and a high ethylene current density of 8.45 mA cm-2. Theoretical calculations show that the dramatically improved catalytic activity and selectivity for ethylene are primarily attributed to the effect of silver composition on copper electronic structure, which increased the number of active sites, reduced the Gibbs free energy. Thus, this work not only offers Ag@Cu Np as a high-performance CO2RR catalyst but also provides insights to guide new electrode design strategies. We believe that this method will benefit the development of other low cost and active electrocatalysts toward large-scale CO2RR applications.
